title: Homeowner directly identifies themselves during registration
description: During account registration, the homeowner provides directly identifying information such as name, email address, phone number, account credentials, or address details to the Home Hub ecosystem. The act of sharing this data identifies the individual to the system.
assumptions: Assumes registration requires account attributes that can directly identify the homeowner.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on standard LINDDUN identification categories; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Enrollment data can link the homeowner to specific devices and household context
description: By enrolling cameras and sensors on the Home Hub, the homeowner shares device identifiers, device types, and household setup information that can be linked to the same account, enabling correlation between the person, their devices, and their home environment.
assumptions: Assumes device enrollment transmits stable device identifiers or serial numbers associated with the registering account.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro sub-node may differ; threat is grounded in linkability between account identity and enrolled devices.

title: Registration and enrollment traffic may disclose sensitive household details in transit
description: Data sent over this flow may reveal privacy-sensitive information such as account details, device serial numbers, camera presence, sensor types, and the existence of a monitored home. If the flow is observable in transit, these contents may be exposed.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries registration and device-enrollment payloads and may be insufficiently protected in transit or observable through local-network interception.
uncertainty_note: Specific node chosen as a generic disclosure-in-transit category; exact sub-node may vary.

title: Flow metadata may link repeated setup actions to the same household
description: Even if payload contents are protected, communication metadata on this flow—such as timing, source endpoint, destination, and repeated enrollment events—may allow an observer to correlate multiple setup actions with the same home or user.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker or third party can observe network metadata for this flow.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort mapping to a metadata-based linkability node; exact node id may differ by catalog version.

title: Home Hub can identify the homeowner through stored account and device enrollment records
description: Upon receiving registration and enrollment data, the Home Hub can associate the homeowner's account with specific cameras and sensors, making the individual and household identifiable within the system.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores or processes account identifiers together with enrolled device records.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may vary; threat reflects identification caused by recipient-side processing.

title: Home Hub learns detailed household monitoring configuration
description: The destination process receives and can infer privacy-sensitive facts about the household, including what rooms or entry points may be monitored, what kinds of sensors are installed, and the security posture of the home.
assumptions: Assumes enrollment includes device type, placement hints, names, or configuration metadata sufficient to infer household characteristics.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node is approximate; disclosure arises from recipient-side processing and storage of enrollment data.

title: Registration and enrollment may occur without sufficiently informed consent or expectation alignment
description: If the Home Hub does not clearly explain what personal data and device metadata are collected, how they are used, and whether they are shared onward, the homeowner may be unaware of the privacy implications of registration and device enrollment.
assumptions: Assumes onboarding notices, consent prompts, or privacy choices may be incomplete or unclear.
uncertainty_note: This depends on product UX and notice design, which are not provided in the flow description.

title: Home Hub may collect more registration or device data than necessary for enrollment
description: The destination process may request or retain excessive personal details or device metadata beyond what is needed to create the account and enroll cameras/sensors, violating data minimization or purpose limitation expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the system could request optional profile data, precise location, or unnecessary device attributes during setup.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the implementation collects unnecessary fields; not certain from the flow description alone.

title: Observation of unlock-code entry reveals guest participation
description: The existence and timing of the communication from the guest to the Home Hub can reveal that a guest is currently attempting access to the home, even without learning the code itself. An observer of the interaction or network traffic may infer the guest's presence or participation.
assumptions: Assumes the code entry or its transmission is observable through local shoulder-surfing, wireless interception, or other side-channel observation.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context gives threat-type applicability but not the detailed node list for this exact case.

title: Temporary access code can identify a specific guest or invitation
description: If the Home Hub treats each temporary access code as unique to a guest, booking, or visit, receipt and processing of the code can identify the guest or single them out within the system.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are unique per guest, stay, or invitation rather than shared generic codes.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate; applicability depends on whether codes are uniquely assigned.

title: Use of the temporary code may link guest access events across time
description: When the Home Hub receives and logs the same temporary code across multiple unlock attempts, it may link separate access events to the same guest or visit, enabling reconstruction of behavior patterns such as arrival times and frequency.
assumptions: Assumes the hub stores or can correlate repeated uses of the same temporary code over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat depends on retention and correlation of code-use events.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having used the temporary code
description: If the Home Hub records successful or failed code submissions together with timestamps, the resulting records can be used as evidence that the guest attempted or performed entry, reducing the guest's plausible deniability.
assumptions: Assumes the hub logs code-entry events and associates them with a unique temporary code or guest context.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; applicability depends on event logging and code uniqueness.

title: Guest may not be aware of logging and secondary use of temporary-code events
description: The Home Hub may process the entered temporary code for purposes beyond immediate authentication, such as storing access logs, monitoring occupancy, or sharing entry events with others, without the guest being adequately informed or given meaningful choice.
assumptions: Assumes the system logs or reuses code-entry data and that notice/consent is absent or insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate because no detailed threat-tree excerpt was provided.

title: Sensor event records can link household activities over time
description: By writing motion, door, and other sensor events into a persistent local log, the Home Hub creates a longitudinal record that can be correlated across timestamps and sensor types to link events to the same household, room, device, or occupant behavior pattern.
assumptions: The event log stores timestamps and sensor/device identifiers, and entries are retained long enough for correlation.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicability by threat type/position, not detailed node ids.

title: Logged sensor events may identify occupants or visitors indirectly
description: Motion and door events, especially when timestamped and associated with specific locations or devices, can reveal presence patterns, arrivals/departures, sleep schedules, and other behavior that may identify or single out residents or frequent visitors even if no explicit names are stored.
assumptions: Sensor identifiers or room context are available in the logged events, enabling inference about specific individuals or small groups.
uncertainty_note: Indirect identifiability depends on household size, sensor placement, and granularity of logged metadata.

title: Local event log stores intimate household behavior data
description: The Local Event Log receives and stores fine-grained motion, door, and sensor events that expose occupancy, routines, absences, and potentially sensitive in-home activities. Persisting these events increases the risk that private behavior becomes observable to anyone with access to the datastore.
assumptions: The datastore retains raw or detailed event histories rather than only short-lived aggregates.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate.

title: Event log may retain more sensor history than necessary
description: If the Local Event Log keeps detailed sensor events indefinitely or at excessive granularity, it can process and retain more personal data than needed for the intended purpose, violating data minimization and storage limitation expectations.
assumptions: There is no strict retention limit, aggregation, or pruning policy for old events.
uncertainty_note: Applies if retention/granularity controls are absent or weak; exact node id is best-effort.

title: Residents may be unaware that detailed in-home events are persistently logged
description: If the system does not clearly communicate that motion, door, and related sensor events are written to a local datastore, data subjects may not understand the extent, persistence, or sensitivity of the monitoring and logging.
assumptions: Users are not explicitly informed in setup, UI, or documentation about the scope and retention of local event logging.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the product's notice and transparency mechanisms, which are not described.

title: Persistent local logging may occur without valid consent or user control
description: If the Local Event Log stores household sensor events by default without an appropriate legal basis, meaningful consent, or an easy way to disable or configure logging, the processing may be non-compliant with privacy obligations.
assumptions: The deployment context requires consent or comparable user control/legal basis for this form of behavioral logging.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on jurisdiction, legal basis, and product controls; exact tree node is approximate.

title: Uploading recorded clips discloses occupants and visitors to a third-party cloud service
description: The Home Hub shares recorded camera clips with cloud storage. Those clips can reveal identifiable people, activities inside or around the home, routines, possessions, and other sensitive contextual information to the cloud provider beyond the local environment.
assumptions: Recorded clips contain personal data such as images, audio, timestamps, or scene context about residents, guests, or passers-by.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided applicability by threat type, not detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Upload traffic metadata can link clips to a specific household or device
description: Even if clip contents are protected, the upload flow may expose metadata such as source IP address, device identifiers, account identifiers, timing, frequency, and clip sizes. This can allow an observer or intermediary to link multiple uploads to the same home, user account, or camera deployment.
assumptions: Network or service metadata is observable by intermediaries, the cloud provider, or other parties with access to transport or application logs.
uncertainty_note: Specific LINDDUN Pro sub-node may differ; using a generic linkability node due to missing detailed tree excerpt.

title: Upload metadata can identify the household behind the camera clips
description: Identifiers carried with the upload, or metadata such as IP address, account token, device serial number, or persistent session information, may enable identification of the resident or household associated with the Home Hub.
assumptions: The upload protocol or surrounding infrastructure exposes stable identifiers or metadata that can be associated with a natural person or household.
uncertainty_note: Specific threat-tree node id is approximate because the provided context did not include detailed identification subtrees.

title: Camera clips and associated metadata are exposed in transit if upload protection is insufficient
description: If the upload channel lacks strong confidentiality protections, the clip contents and metadata may be intercepted during transmission, revealing highly sensitive visual or audio information.
assumptions: Transport encryption, certificate validation, key management, or endpoint trust may be weak or misconfigured.
uncertainty_note: This is a standard disclosure-in-transit threat; exact subtree citation is approximate.

title: Stored clips can be linked across time, cameras, or accounts at the cloud destination
description: Once received by Cloud Video Storage, clips can be aggregated with account data, device identifiers, timestamps, and other stored records, enabling linkage of multiple events and recordings to the same household or individuals over time.
assumptions: The cloud service stores uploads together with persistent account, device, or event metadata.
uncertainty_note: Detailed LINDDUN Pro node id is inferred from general linkability concepts.

title: Cloud storage can identify residents, visitors, or the household from uploaded clips
description: The destination can identify data subjects directly from video or audio content, or indirectly by combining clips with subscriber records, addresses, billing data, and device registration information.
assumptions: Cloud Video Storage is associated with customer account information or other identifying records.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate due to absent detailed tree mapping in the retrieved context.

title: Cloud retention and access to uploaded clips disclose intimate household activities
description: At the destination, storing and processing recorded clips creates a risk that provider personnel, processors, or unauthorized parties with access to the datastore can view or otherwise learn sensitive information about life in and around the home.
assumptions: The cloud environment stores readable clips or can decrypt them, and access controls or internal-use restrictions may be imperfect.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat clearly fits disclosure at destination.

title: Cloud-side analysis of uploaded clips can infer behavior patterns and household characteristics
description: By analyzing stored clips and metadata, the destination may infer occupancy schedules, sleep/work routines, relationships, possessions, health indicators, religious practices, or other private attributes not explicitly provided by the user.
assumptions: The cloud service performs indexing, analytics, AI processing, or operational review over uploaded clips and metadata.
uncertainty_note: Inference is strongly plausible for cloud video storage, but the exact LINDDUN Pro subtree id is approximate.

title: Uploading clips to cloud storage may be non-compliant with data minimization, retention, or lawful-basis requirements
description: Receiving and storing home camera clips in the cloud can create non-compliance risks if the service retains more footage than necessary, lacks an appropriate legal basis, fails to honor purpose limitation, or does not provide required safeguards for bystanders, visitors, or household members.
assumptions: The clips contain personal data subject to privacy regulation or contractual privacy commitments.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine compliance risk, but the exact threat-tree node id is approximate because no detailed compliance subtree was provided.

title: Home Hub may disclose more motion-alert data than necessary to the backend
description: When forwarding a real-time motion alert, the Home Hub may include excessive personal data beyond what is strictly needed for alert handling, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor metadata, or contextual details about occupancy patterns. This creates an avoidable disclosure from the source to another party in the system.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert contains or can be linked to household/person-related data and that some included fields may not be strictly necessary for backend processing.

title: In-transit motion-alert metadata may reveal sensitive occupancy information
description: Even if the payload is limited, the flow itself can disclose personal information through metadata such as alert timing, frequency, routing, device/network identifiers, and association between the Home Hub and backend account. These data can reveal presence-at-home patterns or household activity and therefore constitute implicit disclosure on the data flow.
assumptions: Assumes transport or surrounding infrastructure exposes observable metadata to intermediaries or logs, and that motion alerts are tied to a specific household or user account.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is approximate because the retrieved context explicitly mentions Dd.4 at a high level, not a more specific metadata-focused child node.

title: Backend receipt and storage of real-time motion alerts may overexpose household activity data
description: The Mobile App Backend may process, retain, or make accessible the received motion-alert data to more internal components, operators, or downstream services than necessary. Because motion alerts can reveal behavioral and occupancy patterns, unnecessary retention or broad internal exposure at the destination creates an avoidable data-disclosure threat.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores, logs, republishes, or shares alert contents or related metadata beyond the minimum needed to deliver the mobile notification.

title: Repeated motion-alert transmissions can link events to the same household or user account
description: The recurring flow of real-time motion alerts from a specific Home Hub to the backend can enable linking multiple events to the same household, device, or resident profile. Over time, this supports construction of behavioral patterns such as occupancy schedules or activity rhythms.
assumptions: Assumes stable identifiers, account associations, or persistent network/device metadata are present on the flow or inferable by the backend or intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: The exact LINDDUN Pro child node for linkability was not provided in the retrieved context; L.1 is used as a best-effort generic node.

title: Motion-alert flow may identify a specific household or resident
description: Identifiers carried with or inferable from the alert flow, such as hub ID, account ID, IP address, or routing information, may allow the motion event to be tied to an identifiable household or individual. This turns what might otherwise be event data into identifiable personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the backend or network context can map technical identifiers to a customer account, address, or named user.
uncertainty_note: The exact identifiability tree-node id is not present in the supplied context; I.1 is a best-effort generic node.

title: Notification content may disclose occupancy/activity information beyond necessity
description: By pushing a motion-detected alert to the homeowner, the backend shares inferred in-home activity/occupancy information. If the notification includes detailed text such as exact room, time, or repeated motion events when not strictly necessary, it can disclose sensitive behavioral patterns to the recipient device and anyone able to view notifications on it.
assumptions: Assumes push payload may contain human-readable motion/event details rather than a generic alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Push-notification metadata can link homeowner, device, and motion events
description: Even if notification payload is minimized, the transmission of a push notification can expose metadata such as recipient device token, timing, frequency, and association with a specific home-security app/account. Observers or intermediaries involved in message delivery may link repeated motion alerts to the same homeowner or household.
assumptions: Assumes standard mobile push infrastructure is used and metadata is visible to delivery intermediaries or network observers.
uncertainty_note: Applies mainly to metadata in transit; exact exposure depends on push provider architecture and transport protections.

title: Notification metadata or payload may identify the homeowner or household
description: The flow may contain identifiers such as device tokens, account identifiers, or app-specific routing data. Combined with motion-alert timing, these can identify a particular homeowner, household, or monitored property to parties handling the notification delivery.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers are present in push-routing data or payload and can be associated with a person or address.
uncertainty_note: Identification risk depends on what identifiers are embedded and who can access them during delivery.

title: Notification displayed on the phone may disclose motion events to bystanders
description: Once received, the homeowner's device may display the motion-detected notification on the lock screen, wearable, or notification shade. Anyone with visual access to the device can learn that motion occurred at the home, revealing sensitive information about household activity or security events.
assumptions: Assumes notifications may be shown on lock screen or mirrored to companion devices.
uncertainty_note: Destination-side disclosure depends on user/device notification settings, but this is a common default risk.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of notification visibility and downstream exposure
description: The recipient may not understand that motion alerts can appear on lock screens, wearables, shared devices, or notification histories, creating an unawareness risk about how far the event information is exposed after receipt.
assumptions: Assumes the app or platform does not clearly explain notification privacy settings and exposure surfaces.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement mapping to unawareness; exact applicability depends on UX and privacy notices.

title: Backend may send motion notifications without sufficiently specific consent or preference control
description: If the backend pushes motion-detected alerts by default, or without granular user preferences for content, timing, and channels, the sharing of event information may exceed the homeowner's consent or expectations.
assumptions: Assumes notification preferences/consent may be bundled, default-enabled, or insufficiently granular.
uncertainty_note: Consent/compliance impact depends on jurisdiction and actual preference-management design.

title: Aggregated analytics may still enable linkage across sessions or cohorts before disclosure
description: The mobile app backend shares aggregated device-usage analytics with the cloud analytics vendor. Even when data is described as aggregated, stable dimensions, small cohorts, repeated reporting windows, or persistent device/app attributes can allow the vendor to link records across time, products, or datasets.
assumptions: Assumes the aggregation may retain stable keys, fine-grained dimensions, or repeated cohort breakdowns that permit correlation.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Shared analytics may permit inference of individual or device identity despite aggregation
description: If the backend discloses analytics with sparse segments, rare usage patterns, quasi-identifiers, or fine temporal/geographic granularity, the cloud analytics vendor may be able to identify a user or device, or single one out, from the supposedly aggregated dataset.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity-style controls, or suppression of rare groups are absent or insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Identification risk depends strongly on actual aggregation design and auxiliary data available to the vendor.

title: Disclosure of sensitive usage patterns to the analytics vendor
description: Device-usage analytics can reveal behavioral patterns, app engagement, feature use, time-of-day habits, or other potentially sensitive information. Sending these analytics to an external vendor exposes that information beyond the original service boundary.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics contain meaningful behavioral or contextual signals, even if aggregated.
uncertainty_note: Exact sensitivity depends on the analytics fields included.

title: Vendor may use received analytics beyond the original purpose
description: Once the cloud analytics vendor receives the analytics, it may retain, repurpose, combine, or analyze them for broader product improvement, benchmarking, profiling, or other secondary uses not aligned with the original purpose for which the backend collected the data.
assumptions: Assumes contractual, technical, or organizational purpose-limitation controls are incomplete or weak.
uncertainty_note: Applies unless strong processor-only restrictions and enforcement are in place.

title: Users may be unaware that analytics are shared with an external vendor
description: If the app's privacy notices, in-product disclosures, or consent flows do not clearly explain that aggregated device-usage analytics are sent to a cloud analytics vendor, users may lack awareness of this external disclosure and processing.
assumptions: Assumes transparency notices are incomplete, unclear, or not presented at the relevant time.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine risk for this flow, but whether it materializes depends on the actual notice and UX.

title: Sharing analytics with the vendor may occur without a valid legal basis or user choice
description: The backend's disclosure of device-usage analytics to an external analytics vendor may require consent, legitimate-interest balancing, opt-out support, or another lawful basis depending on jurisdiction and the nature of the analytics. If these conditions are not met, the sharing is non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy law or policy imposes conditions on third-party analytics sharing.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations vary by jurisdiction and by whether the data is truly anonymized versus merely aggregated/pseudonymized.

title: Linkability via retrieval metadata on the video-fetch flow
description: The retrieval flow can expose metadata such as homeowner account identifier, device/app identifier, clip identifier, timestamps, IP address, and access patterns. Observers of the flow or intermediaries with access to logs may correlate repeated fetches to the same homeowner, household, camera, or event history, linking separate playback actions together.
assumptions: Applies if network/intermediary/application logs or transport metadata are accessible beyond strictly authorized components, even if payload content is protected.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context did not include the specific Linkability subtree for this interaction.

title: Identifiability of the homeowner through video retrieval traffic
description: The flow may reveal the identity of a specific homeowner or household because the requested clip and associated metadata can be tied to an account, property, camera, or device. Even without full payload inspection, request metadata may permit singling out the user performing playback.
assumptions: Applies where request metadata, identifiers, or routing information are visible to parties beyond those strictly needing it.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifiability node citation is approximate; applicability depends on what identifiers are present in the request/response and logs.

title: Backend learns sensitive inferences from requested video clips
description: By retrieving and handling stored clips for playback, the mobile app backend can infer occupancy patterns, routines, visitors, incidents, and other intimate household behaviors from the clip requested and the timing/frequency of playback. This exceeds mere transport and arises from the backend's processing of the received video and associated metadata.
assumptions: Applies if P2 can inspect clip content or rich metadata, or if access logs are retained and analyzed.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node is selected by best judgement because the retrieved context did not provide the Detectability/Disclosure subtree details.

title: Disclosure of personal video data at the backend
description: The backend receives highly sensitive personal data in the form of home video footage. If P2 stores, caches, logs, or otherwise exposes the clip or its metadata beyond what is necessary for immediate playback, unauthorized parties or internal roles may gain access to intimate household information.
assumptions: Applies especially if clips are cached server-side, copied into diagnostics, or made accessible to support/operations personnel.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subtree citation is approximate; the general disclosure threat clearly applies to backend receipt and handling of video data.

title: Secondary use of retrieved video beyond playback
description: Once the backend retrieves the clip, it may be used for purposes beyond the homeowner's immediate playback request, such as analytics, model training, employee review, troubleshooting archives, or law-enforcement sharing, without the data subject's expectation or valid basis. The privacy threat arises from what P2 does with the data on receipt.
assumptions: Applies if governance or technical controls do not strictly limit use to the requested playback function.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context did not include the Unawareness subtree.

title: Storage limitation violation for retrieved video at the backend
description: The backend may retain fetched clips, thumbnails, transcoded derivatives, or access logs longer than necessary for playback, violating storage limitation obligations. This is a non-compliance threat caused by P2's retention behavior after receiving the video.
assumptions: Includes temporary caches, backups, observability pipelines, and support artifacts if retention is not bounded and justified.
